Monday, 3 July, evening. Julien and Karim are having a drink on a terrace by the Saône. There are twelve days left until Marchand’s deadline.
So, Paris? Although you didn’t tell me anything, I guessed straight away. You’ve got the face of someone who doesn’t sleep any more.
However much I think about it, I can’t decide. The post is extraordinary. And yet something is holding me back.
Something or someone? Ioana, Rose-Hélène, Hélène, Odile… even if you leave, they’ll always be here, you know.
I know. But Ioana is going to become a partner in her firm, whereas I would force her to start all over again from zero.
I left for Montréal at twenty-five, despite the opinion of my whole family. And I came back five years later.
Not at all. Although it’s hard to leave, I learned a lot there. On the other hand, I was alone. You have a family.
There’s something else. Marchand told me a project was being prepared here, in Lyon. I called the Conservatoire this morning. The director wants to see me on Thursday.
And you’re only telling me now? Instead of talking about Paris for an hour!
Because it isn’t certain at all. The project depends on funding from the region. Whereas Paris is signed, or almost.
Listen. Even if it’s uncertain, go and see her anyway. Whatever happens, at least you’ll know what you’re turning down.
You’re right. Although I don’t like waiting, I’ll wait until Thursday before answering Marchand.
And Ioana, what does she think?
She says she’ll follow me, even to the end of the world. Despite that, I can see she’s afraid. And so am I.
(raises his glass) Then, to Thursday. And to the decision you’ll make together, whatever it may be.

1. Bien que + subjunctive, même si + indicative
Both mean "although / even if", but they take DIFFERENT moods. It’s a classic trap:
Bien que ce soit dur, j’ai appris beaucoup.
Même si tu pars, ils seront toujours là.
Although you didn’t tell me anything, I guessed.
Even if it’s uncertain, go and see her.
Common mistakes: "bien que c’est" (correct: "bien que ce SOIT") and "même si ce soit" (correct: "même si c’EST"). Trick: "que" takes the subjunctive, "si" takes the indicative — as in chapter 42.
"Malgré" (despite) is a PREPOSITION: it is followed by a noun or a pronoun, never by a conjugated verb:
Despite the opinion of my whole family, I left.
Despite that, I can see she’s afraid.
"Malgré que" + subjunctive exists in speech, but it is considered wrong in writing. Use "bien que".
Le poste est extraordinaire. Pourtant, quelque chose me retient.
all the same, anyway (at the end, spoken)
J’ai beau réfléchir, je n’arrive pas à décider.
"Avoir beau" is conjugated: j’ai beau, tu as beau, il a beau… "Elle a beau crier, personne ne l’entend." = However much she shouts, nobody hears her.
4. Contrast: alors que, tandis que, en revanche, au lieu de
These expressions set two different facts against each other:
Ioana will become a partner, whereas I would force her to start again.
The project is uncertain, whereas Paris is signed.
I learned a lot there. On the other hand, I was alone.
Instead of talking about Paris, talk to me about Lyon!
"Alors que" and "tandis que" are followed by the indicative. "Au lieu de" is followed by an infinitive or a noun.
They’re very elegant in writing. "Quoi qu’il arrive" is the most used in speech.
However much I think about it, I don’t know.
She likes tea, whereas he prefers coffee.
"Even if it rains, I’m going out."

On Thursday 6 July, at ten o’clock, Julien walked into the Lyon Conservatoire, a large old building on the banks of the Saône. Although he had walked past it hundreds of times, he had never been inside. He had put on the white shirt embroidered "3 May", for luck.

The director, Claire Vasseur, was waiting for him in her office, a room full of scores and green plants. She was a small, energetic woman with very short grey hair, who talked fast and laughed loudly. She shook his hand as if she had known him forever.

"Olivier told me everything," she began. "He may have lived in Paris for fifteen years, but he’s never forgotten Lyon. And he thinks you deserve to choose knowing all the possibilities. So here’s mine."

She unfolded a large map of the city on the table. Red circles surrounded several neighbourhoods: Vaulx-en-Velin, La Duchère, Vénissieux. "In these neighbourhoods," she explained, "many children have never touched an instrument, even though they have as much talent as the others."

The project was called "Music for All". The Conservatoire wanted to create a department to train teachers able to teach in these neighbourhoods, and to launch children’s orchestras in schools. "I need someone to run it. Someone who knows how to talk to children. Like you."

Then she became serious. "I’ll be honest. Although I have the city’s support, nothing is signed. The region will vote on the funding in December. If it says no, there will be no project. And even if it says yes, the salary will be lower than in Paris. Much lower."

"On the other hand," she added with a smile, "you could start in September, part-time, with a small pilot orchestra. You’d keep your pupils in the Croix-Rousse. And you’d come home for dinner every evening."

Julien left the Conservatoire with his head full of music and questions. He walked for a long time along the Saône, as far as the Saint-Georges footbridge. Paris meant prestige, security, a comfortable salary. Lyon was a new dream, but an uncertain one, which could vanish in December.

That same day, Nathalie had handed Ioana an official letter. She was offering to make her a partner from 1 January, with her name on the door of the firm, next to her own. Ioana had read it three times in the toilets, so that no one would see her cry. Then she had asked for time: until 15 July.

"The fifteenth of July?" said Nathalie, raising an eyebrow. "It seems to be an important date for both of you." Ioana just nodded. Nathalie didn’t ask any questions. She said: "Take your time. But know that, whatever you decide, this letter will remain valid."

On Saturday, the whole family helped Radu and Lucia repaint their studio under the roof. It was thirty-two degrees. Despite the heat, the atmosphere was cheerful: Lucia was singing flamenco, Karim had brought pizzas, and Leïla was running the operation with a roller in her hand.

Radu, on the other hand, was a disaster. He had more paint on his face than on the walls. At one point he knocked a whole pot of yellow paint over his feet. "Although he’s the worst painter in the world," said Lucia, laughing, "I love him all the same." Radu answered by putting yellow on her nose.

That evening, on the way home, Julien bumped into Odile on the stairs. She was coming back from the market, a basket of cherries on her arm. She looked at him for a moment, then put her basket down on a step. "Have you got a minute, Julien? I have something to tell you. Ioana told me."

They both sat down on the steps, like two teenagers. "You know Henri was a sailor," Odile began. "After Algeria, he chose the sea, to run away. We were happy, truly. And yet, for forty years, there was always a part of him somewhere else. In a piano, in Lyon."

"I’m not telling you to stay," she went on. "Or to leave. I’m only telling you this: whatever your choice, make it completely. Don’t leave a part of yourself in Paris if you stay, or in Lyon if you leave. Otherwise you’ll spend your life whistling a waltz nobody hears."

She stood up, picked up her basket and gave him a handful of cherries. Julien stayed sitting on the steps long after she had gone in, the cherries in his hand, without eating them. Upstairs, he could hear Ioana singing a Romanian lullaby.

The next day, Julien gave Théo his last lesson of the year. The boy noticed at once that his teacher was distracted. "You’re going to leave, aren’t you?" he asked abruptly. "My mother says good teachers always end up leaving for Paris." Julien didn’t know what to answer.

"Even if you leave," Théo went on, looking at his hands, "I’ll keep on with the piano. But I’d rather you stayed. Even though you’re very strict about scales." Julien laughed in spite of himself. Then he had him play the waltz one last time, without correcting anything.

On 14 July, as the year before, they went up to Fourvière to see the fireworks. But this time they watched them from the terrace of the care home, with Hélène, Madame Lambert, Monsieur Petit and about twenty residents settled in their armchairs, blankets on their knees despite the heat.

Ioana remembered last year: the same café terrace, the same view, and that strange queasiness, the smell of coffee that disgusted her. It was the evening she had begun to suspect she was pregnant. A year later, Rose-Hélène was asleep in her arms, despite the explosions.

Monsieur Petit commented on every rocket like a football match. Madame Lambert corrected his grammar. Hélène, for her part, wasn’t looking at the sky. She was looking at Julien. At the end, when the last rocket had faded, she beckoned him over.
"I won’t ask you anything," she murmured. "But whatever you decide, come and tell me yourself. Not on the phone. Here, on this bench. Henri never told me. And I waited sixty years to find out."

That evening, Ioana and Julien stayed out on their balcony very late. The city smelled of gunpowder and summer. They went over everything one last time: Paris and Lyon, Marchand and Claire Vasseur, Nathalie and her letter, Hélène, Odile, Radu, the nursery, the cat, the waltz.

"Although I’m afraid," said Ioana, "I’ll follow you. I really mean it." Julien took her hand. "And I, even if it’s the dream of my life, don’t want a dream in which you’re sad. However hard I look, I can’t find any music worth that."

They fell silent. Down in the street, some young people were walking home singing. Somewhere, one last firecracker went off. Then Ioana said softly: "Tomorrow is the fifteenth." Julien nodded. "Tomorrow morning," he said, "we’ll decide. Together."

Dear Dad and Mum, I’ve been in Montréal for three months. Although you were against my leaving, I’m writing to tell you I’m well.
It’s minus twenty degrees. Despite the cold, the city is magnificent: everything is white, and people skate on the frozen lakes, whereas in Lyon we complain as soon as it’s five degrees.
My job is fascinating, even if my colleagues make fun of my accent. Here, I’m the one who talks funny! They say "char" instead of "voiture", and they think it’s normal.

I don’t know if I’ll stay long. On the other hand, I know one thing: whatever happens, I’ll never regret having left. I needed to see the world.
Give my sisters a kiss. And Mum, send me the couscous recipe, even though I know mine will never be as good as yours. Your loving son, Karim.
